Package org.jdesktop.lg3d.mandela.values

Class Operators

java.lang.Object
org.jdesktop.lg3d.mandela.values.Operators
public final class Operators extends Object
The operator meanings: what +, /, [i] and .length do to the values the machine puts in front of them.

These rules live here rather than inside the interpreter loop for two reasons: the machine stays a fetch/decode/dispatch shell that is easy to read and to step through in a debugger, and every rule below is testable headlessly without building a script or a runtime. The language guide's operator table is written from this file, so the two cannot drift apart.

Numbers. Mandela has one integer type (Int, a long) and one floating type (Double). An operation on two integers stays an integer unless it would overflow, in which case it is promoted to Double rather than wrapping: a desktop script that silently rolls over at 2^63 is worse than one that loses precision. Division of two integers is exact when it divides (6 / 3 is 2), and a Double otherwise.

Null. No operator except ==, != and ?? accepts null; each rejection is a NullError naming the operation, which is the single most common script bug and therefore worth a specific message.

  • Method Details

    • add

      public static Object add(Object left, Object right)
      a + b: numeric sum, textual concatenation, or the union of two collections.

      The three forms are chosen by the operands agreeing, never by one side being silently converted: 1 + "x" is an error rather than "1x", so a value that reached the wrong branch of a script fails at the concatenation instead of building a plausible-looking string. Write str(x) or interpolation when a conversion is intended.

    • concat

      public static Object concat(Object left, Object right)
      Join two values as text, rendering each with its display form. This is what an interpolation compiles to: "n=${n}" accepts any value, while the + operator stays strict so a mistyped concatenation fails loudly.

    • index

      public static Object index(Object target, Object key)
      target[key].

      Lists accept negative indices counting from the end, maps are keyed by text, ranges test membership, strings index by code point and an instance answers its field names, so one opcode reaches every container the language has.

    • contains

      public static boolean contains(Object value, Object container)
      value in container: membership, which is not the same question as indexing.

      A list answers with Mandela equality, so 1.0 in [1] is true exactly when 1.0 == 1 is; a map is named by text and searched by its keys, not its values; a string looks for a substring; and a range answers arithmetically, which is what keeps 7 in 0..1000000 step 7 free. Anything else is not a container, and saying so is the point: x in 5 is a mistake, not a false.
